paragraphs.text: 1.1. I, Chariton of Aphrodisias, secretary to the orator Athenagoras, am about to relate a love story that took place in Syracuse. Hermocrates, the general of the Syracusans, the man who defeated the Athenians, had a daughter named Callirhoe, a marvel of a girl and the glory of all Sicily.

1.2. For her beauty was not human but divine, and not that of a Nereid or a mountain nymph but of Aphrodite herself. Word of this astonishing sight ran everywhere, and suitors poured into Syracuse, princes and the sons of tyrants, not from Sicily alone but from Italy and Epirus and the islands off Epirus as well.

1.3. But Love wished to join a couple of his own choosing. There was a young man named Chaereas, handsome, surpassing all others, such as sculptors and painters represent Achilles and Nireus and Hippolytus and Alcibiades. His father was Ariston, the second man in Syracuse after Hermocrates. And there was a certain political rivalry between the two families, so that they would sooner have made a marriage alliance with anyone else than with each other.
1.4. But Love is fond of strife and delights in unexpected triumphs, and he looked for an occasion of this kind. There was a public festival of Aphrodite, and nearly all the women went to her temple.

1.5. Callirhoe had not been out of doors until then, but her mother brought her forward, since Hermocrates had ordered her to make her devotions to the goddess. At that very moment Chaereas was walking home from the wrestling-grounds, shining like a star; for the flush of the palaestra blossomed on the brightness of his face like gold upon silver.

1.6. So by chance, meeting at a rather narrow turning, they ran into each other, the god having arranged this encounter so that each might be seen by the other. At once they exchanged a passion of love . . .

1.7. Chaereas could barely make his way home with his wound, like a brave man struck by a mortal blow in battle, ashamed to fall yet unable to stand, for the beauty had pierced him to the heart. And the girl fell at the feet of Aphrodite and, kissing them, said, "Mistress, give me this man whom you have shown me."

1.8. A dreadful night came upon them both, for the fire was kindled. But the girl suffered the more grievously through her silence, ashamed to be found out. Chaereas, however, a young man of noble nature and high spirit, now that his body was wasting away, brought himself to tell his parents that he was in love and would not live unless he won marriage with Callirhoe.

1.9. His father groaned when he heard it and said, "You are lost to me, my child; for it is plain that Hermocrates would never give you his daughter when he has so many wealthy and royal suitors. You must not even make the attempt, lest we be openly insulted." So the father tried to comfort the boy, but his trouble only grew, until he no longer even went out to his usual haunts.

1.10. The gymnasium missed Chaereas and was as it were deserted, for the young men loved him. Inquiring closely into the cause, they learned of his sickness, and pity for the handsome youth came over them all, that he was in danger of perishing through a passion of his noble soul.

1.11. A lawful assembly was convened. The people, sitting in session, before anything else and as their only cry, shouted, "Noble Hermocrates, great general, save Chaereas! This shall be the first of your trophies. The city is suing for the marriage—

1.12. today—of two who are worthy of each other." Who could describe that assembly, of which Love himself was the popular leader? Hermocrates, a man who loved his city, could not refuse the city's plea. When he had given his assent, the whole people leapt up out of the theater, and the young men hurried off to Chaereas, while the council and the magistrates followed Hermocrates.

1.13. The women of Syracuse were also present at his house, escorting the bride. The wedding-hymn was sung throughout the city; the streets were full of garlands and torches; the doorways were sprinkled with wine and perfume. The Syracusans spent this day more joyfully than the day of their victory celebrations.

1.14. The girl, knowing nothing of all this, lay thrown upon her bed with her face covered, weeping and silent. Her nurse came to the couch and said, "Child, get up; the day most longed for by us all is here. The city is escorting you as a bride." At this her knees and her heart gave way, for she did not know to whom she was being married. At once she was speechless, and darkness poured over her eyes, and she almost gave up her breath; but those who saw it took this for modesty.

1.15. When the maidservants had quickly dressed her, the crowd left the doors, and the parents brought the bridegroom in to the girl. Chaereas ran forward and kissed her, and Callirhoe, recognizing her beloved, like the flame of a lamp already dying down when oil is poured upon it, blazed up again and grew greater and stronger.

1.16. When she came forth into public view, amazement seized the whole crowd, as when Artemis appears to hunters in a lonely place; and many of those present even fell down in worship. They all marveled at Callirhoe and counted Chaereas blessed. Just so the poets celebrate the wedding of Thetis, which took place on Pelion. Yet here too some malicious spirit was found, as they say Strife was found there.

2.1. For the suitors who had failed to win the marriage felt grief mingled with anger. Though until then they had been at odds with one another, now they were of one mind, and out of this concord, thinking themselves insulted, they came together to a common council; and it was envy that enlisted them for the war against Chaereas.

2.2. First a young Italian rose, the son of the tyrant of Rhegium, and spoke as follows: "If one of us had married her, I would not have been angry, just as in the athletic contests one of the competitors must win; but since the man who took no trouble at all for the marriage has outshone us, I cannot bear the insult.

2.3. We have worn ourselves out keeping watch before the courtyard doors, flattering nurses and maidservants and sending gifts to her attendants. How long we have been slaves! And, hardest of all, we have hated one another as rivals; while this whore-monger, this pauper, this man no better than anyone, when kings were competing, has carried off the crown without a struggle.

2.4. But let the prize do him no good, and let us make his marriage death to the bridegroom." All approved, except the tyrant of Acragas, who spoke against it. "It is not out of goodwill toward Chaereas," he said, "that I forbid the plot, but out of safer calculation. For remember that Hermocrates is not a man to despise; so open war against him is beyond us, but craft is the stronger course.

2.5. Indeed, it is by cunning rather than force that we win tyrannies. Elect me general for the war against Chaereas. I promise to break up the marriage; for I will arm jealousy against him, and jealousy, taking love as its ally, will work some great evil.

2.6. Now Callirhoe is steady and untouched by any malicious suspicion, while Chaereas, raised as he was in the gymnasium and not without experience of youthful faults, can easily be made to suspect and so fall into the jealousy of a lover; and it is easier, too, to approach him and to talk with him." While he was still speaking, they all voted for his proposal and put the business into his hands, as a man competent to contrive anything. And so he set about a scheme of this kind.

3.1. It was evening, and a man came with news that Ariston, Chaereas's father, had fallen from a ladder on the farm and had very little hope of life. When Chaereas heard it, though he loved his father, still he was grieved chiefly because he would have to go away alone; for it was not yet possible to take the girl out with him.

3.2. On that very night no one ventured to hold a revel openly, but men came in secret and unseen and left the signs of a revel: they garlanded the doorway, sprinkled it with perfumes, made mud of wine, and threw down half-burnt torches.

3.3. Day broke, and every passerby stopped, moved by that common impulse of curiosity. Chaereas, his father being now somewhat recovered, was hurrying to his wife. Seeing the crowd before the doors, at first he was astonished; but when he learned the cause, he rushed in beside himself.

3.4. Finding the bedchamber still locked, he beat upon it eagerly. When the maidservant opened, he fell upon Callirhoe, and his anger turned to grief, and tearing his clothes he wept. When she asked what had happened, he was speechless, unable either to disbelieve what he had seen or to believe what he did not wish to.

3.5. As he stood at a loss and trembling, his wife, suspecting nothing of what had happened, begged him to tell her the reason for his trouble. But he, with bloodshot eyes and a harsh voice, said, "I am weeping for my own fortune, because you have forgotten me so quickly," and he reproached her with the revel.

3.6. But she, as the daughter of a general and full of spirit, was stung by the unjust accusation and said, "No one held a revel at my father's house; but your doorway is perhaps used to revels, and your marriage grieves your lovers." With these words she turned away and, covering her face, let fall streams of tears.

3.7. But reconciliations come easily to lovers, and they gladly accept any excuse from each other. So Chaereas, changing his mood, began to coax her, and his wife quickly welcomed his repentance. This only inflamed their love the more, and the parents of both counted themselves blessed to see the harmony of their children.

4.1. The man from Acragas, his first device having failed, now turned to a more effective contrivance, something of this kind. He had a parasite, a smooth talker, full of every social charm. This man he ordered to play the part of a lover; for he set him to win the favor of Callirhoe's personal maid, the most valued of her attendants.

4.2. It was hard work, but at last he won the girl over with lavish gifts and by saying that he would hang himself if he did not get his desire. And a woman is easily caught when she thinks herself loved. Having thus laid his groundwork, the contriver of the drama found a second actor, no longer so charming, but cunning and convincing in speech.

4.3. Instructing this man beforehand in what he must do and say, he sent him to Chaereas as a stranger. The man approached him as he was idling about the wrestling-grounds and said, "I too had a son, Chaereas, of your own age, who greatly admired and loved you while he lived. Since his death I look on you as my own son, for you are a common blessing to all Sicily in your good fortune.

4.4. Give me, then, a little of your leisure, and you shall hear great matters that concern your whole life." With such words that vile man lifted up the boy's spirit and filled him with hope and fear and curiosity; and when Chaereas begged him to speak, he hesitated and made the excuse that the present moment was not suitable, that he needed delay and a longer leisure.

4.5. Chaereas pressed him the harder, now expecting something more serious; and the man, taking him by the right hand, led him off to a quiet place, then knitting his brows and looking like a man in distress, and shedding a few tears, said, "It is with reluctance, Chaereas, that I reveal to you a painful matter; I have long wished to speak but held back. But now that you are openly insulted and the dreadful thing is talked of everywhere, I cannot bear to keep silent; for by nature I hate wickedness, and I am especially well disposed toward you.

4.6. Know, then, that your wife is committing adultery, and so that you may believe it, I am ready to show you the adulterer in the very act." So he spoke; and a black cloud of grief enveloped Chaereas, and with both hands he took up the dark dust and poured it over his head, and disfigured his handsome face.

4.7. For a long while he lay speechless, unable to open his mouth or lift his eyes; but when he had gathered a voice, unlike his own and faint, he said, "It is an unhappy favor I ask of you, to be the eyewitness of my own misfortunes; yet show me, so that I may make away with myself the more reasonably. For I will spare Callirhoe even if she has wronged me."

4.8. "Pretend," said the man, "to go off to the farm, but late in the evening keep watch on the house; for you will see the adulterer go in." They agreed on this, and Chaereas, sending word—for he could not endure even to go in himself—said, "I am going off to the farm." But that malicious slanderer was arranging the scene.

4.9. So when evening came on, Chaereas went to his place of watch, and the other, having corrupted Callirhoe's maid, sent into the alley a man pretending to be one bent on secret deeds, but contriving everything so as not to go unnoticed. He had glistening hair and locks dripping with perfume, his eyes painted, a soft cloak, a delicate sandal; heavy rings glittered upon him. Then, after looking about him at length, he approached the door, knocked lightly, and gave the usual signal.

4.10. The maidservant, herself in great fear, quietly opened a little and, taking him by the hand, led him in. When Chaereas saw this, he could restrain himself no longer but rushed in to kill the adulterer in the very act.

4.11. But the man, who had taken his stand by the courtyard door, slipped out at once. Callirhoe, meanwhile, was sitting on the bed, longing for Chaereas, and had not even lit a lamp in her grief. When she heard the sound of footsteps, she was the first to recognize her husband's breathing, and rejoicing she ran to him.

4.12. But he had no voice with which to upbraid her, and overcome by his anger he kicked her as she came toward him. The foot, well aimed, struck against her diaphragm and stopped the girl's breath, and as she lay there the maidservants lifted her up and laid her on the couch.

5.1. So Callirhoe lay speechless and breathless, presenting to all the likeness of a corpse, while Rumor, the messenger of the calamity, ran through the whole city, raising a wail through the streets all the way to the sea; and on every side the lamentation was heard, and the thing was like the capture of a city. Chaereas, still seething with rage, shut himself in all night long and tortured the maidservants, the personal maid first and last.

5.2. While they were still being burned and cut, he learned the truth. Then pity came over him for the dead woman, and he longed to kill himself; but Polycharmus prevented him, a chosen friend such as Homer made Patroclus to Achilles. When day came, the magistrates drew lots for a court to try the killer, hastening the trial out of regard for Hermocrates.

5.3. And the whole people ran together into the marketplace, with different men shouting different things; and the disappointed suitors played the demagogue, and the man from Acragas above all the rest, brilliant and exultant, as one who had accomplished a deed that no one would have expected.

5.4. And a strange thing happened, such as had never before been done in a court of law: when the accusation had been delivered, the killer, with the water measured out to him, instead of making his defense accused himself more bitterly and was the first to cast the condemning vote, saying nothing of what justice would have allowed for his defense—not the slander, not the jealousy, not that the act was involuntary—but he begged them all: "Stone me to death in public; I have stripped the people of their crown.

5.5. It would be a kindness if you handed me over to the executioner. This I would have deserved to suffer even if I had killed a maidservant of Hermocrates. Seek out some unspeakable manner of punishment. I have done worse than temple-robbers and parricides. Do not bury me, do not defile the earth, but sink my impious body in the sea."

5.6. As he spoke, a wail broke out, and all, leaving the dead woman, mourned for the living man. Hermocrates was the first to speak in Chaereas's defense. "I know," he said, "that what happened was involuntary. I see those who are plotting against us. They shall not gloat over two corpses,

5.7. nor will I grieve my dead daughter. I have often heard her say that she wished Chaereas to live rather than herself. So let us put an end to this needless trial and proceed to the burial that cannot be avoided. Let us not surrender the dead woman to time, nor make the body unsightly by delay. Let us bury Callirhoe while she is still beautiful."

6.1. So the judges cast the acquitting vote, but Chaereas would not acquit himself; he longed for death and contrived every means to his end. Polycharmus, seeing there was no other way to save him, said, "Traitor to the dead woman, will you not even endure to bury Callirhoe? Do you entrust her body to other men's hands? Now is the time for you to see to the costliness of her burial and to prepare a royal funeral procession." This argument persuaded him,

6.2. for it instilled in him ambition and care. Who, then, could fittingly describe that funeral procession? Callirhoe lay clothed in bridal dress upon a gilded bier, greater and lovelier than ever, so that all likened her to the sleeping Ariadne.

6.3. Before the bier went first the Syracusan horsemen, themselves and their horses in full array; after these came hoplites bearing the standards of Hermocrates's trophies; then the council, and in the midst of the people all the citizens escorting Hermocrates as a bodyguard. Ariston too was carried along, still sick, calling Callirhoe his daughter and his mistress. After these came the women of the citizens, dressed in black,

6.4. then a royal wealth of grave-offerings: first the gold and silver of the dowry, the beauty and adornment of garments—and Hermocrates sent much from the spoils of war—and the gifts of kinsmen and friends, and last the wealth of Chaereas; for he longed, if it were possible, to burn up his whole estate with his wife.

6.5. The young men of Syracuse bore the bier, and the multitude followed. While all were lamenting, Chaereas was heard above the rest. There was a magnificent tomb of Hermocrates near the sea, so that it was conspicuous even to those sailing far off at sea; this, like a treasury, the costliness of the grave-offerings filled. But what seemed to have been done in honor of the dead woman set in motion the beginning of greater events.

7.1. There was a man named Theron, a scoundrel, who sailed the sea out of wickedness and kept pirates lurking about the harbors. Under the name of a ferryboat he was assembling a pirate band; and being present at the funeral, he cast a covetous eye on the gold, and at night could not sleep upon his bed, saying to himself, "Here am I, risking my life in fighting the sea and killing living men for small gains, when it is possible to grow rich from a single corpse. Let the die be cast; I will not let the profit go. But whom shall I enlist for the venture? Consider, Theron, which of the men you know is fit. Zenophanes of Thurii? Shrewd, but a coward. Menon of Messene? Bold, but a traitor." Running over each in his mind, like an assayer of silver, and rejecting many, he nevertheless settled on certain suitable men. At dawn, then, hurrying down to the harbor, he sought each one out. He found some in brothels, others in taverns—an army fit for such a general. Saying he had something necessary to discuss with them, he led them off behind the harbor and began this speech: "I have found a treasure, and out of all men I chose you as my partners; for the profit is not for one man, nor does it call for much labor, but a single night can make us all rich. We are not without experience of such enterprises, which among foolish men have a bad name but give profit to the sensible." They understood at once that he was proposing piracy or tomb-robbing or temple-robbing, and they said, "Stop—you are dealing with men already convinced; only tell us the deed, and let us not waste the moment." Theron, taking up the thread, said, "You have seen the gold and silver of the dead woman. This would more justly belong to us, the living. I propose that we open the tomb by night, then load the goods aboard the cutter, sail wherever the wind takes us, and sell off the cargo in a foreign land." It pleased them. "For now," he said, "go off to your usual haunts; but late in the evening let each man come down to the cutter, bringing a builder's tool."

8.1. So they were busy with these things; but as for Callirhoe, she experienced a kind of second rebirth, and when, after her starvation, some relaxation came to her arrested breathing, she revived slowly and little by little. Then she began to move her body limb by limb, and opening her eyes she had the sensation of one waking from sleep, and she called for Chaereas as though he lay beside her.

8.2. But when neither her husband nor the maidservants answered, and all was desolation and darkness, a shudder and trembling seized the girl, who could not by reasoning grasp the truth. Slowly rousing herself, she touched the garlands and ribbons and made a clinking of gold and silver; and there was a strong fragrance of spices.

8.3. Then she remembered the kick and the fall it had caused, and at last, out of her agony, she understood the tomb. She broke into a cry, as loud as she could: "Save me, help me!" But when, though she cried out many times, nothing more came of it, she now despaired of rescue and, sinking her head upon her knees, she lamented, saying, "Alas for my miseries! I have been buried alive, though I have done no wrong, and I am dying a lingering death.

8.4. They are mourning me while I am in good health. Whom will anyone send as a messenger? Unjust Chaereas, I blame you not because you killed me, but because you hastened to cast me out of the house. You should not have buried Callirhoe so quickly, and not truly dead. But already, perhaps, you are planning another marriage."

9.1. And while she was thus in her varied laments, Theron, waiting for the very middle of the night, came up noiselessly to the tomb, touching the sea lightly with his oars. Stepping out, he first assigned each man his task.

9.2. He sent four to keep watch, in case anyone should approach the place—to kill them if they could, and if not, to signal their arrival by a sign; and he himself made the fifth to go up to the tomb. The rest—for they were sixteen in all—he ordered to remain on the cutter and to keep the oars poised, so that, if anything sudden should happen, they might quickly snatch up the men from the land and sail away.

9.3. When the crowbars had been brought up and a more violent blow struck to break open the tomb, Callirhoe was seized all at once by everything—fear, joy, grief, wonder, hope, disbelief. "Where is the sound from? Is some divinity, by the common law of the dying, coming for me in my wretchedness? Or is it not a sound, but the voice of those beneath the earth calling me to them? It is more likely to be tomb-robbers; for this too has been added to my misfortunes: wealth is useless

9.4. to a corpse." While she was still reasoning thus, the robber thrust in his head and slowly crept inside. Callirhoe fell at his feet, wishing to make her plea; and he, terrified, leapt out and, trembling, cried to his comrades, "Let us flee from here; for some divinity guards the place within and will not let us enter." Theron laughed at him,

9.5. calling him a coward and more dead than the dead woman, and then he ordered another to go in. When no one would, he himself went in, holding his sword before him. As the iron flashed, Callirhoe, afraid she would be killed, stretched herself into the corner and from there entreated him, sending out a faint voice: "Have pity, whoever you are, on one who has not been pitied by husband or parents; do not kill her whom you have saved."

9.6. At this Theron took more courage, and as a clever man he understood the truth. He stood thoughtful, and at first he resolved to kill the woman, thinking she would be an obstacle to the whole enterprise; but a swift change of mind came over him because of the profit, and he said to himself, "Let her too be part of the grave-offerings; there is much silver here and much gold, but more precious than all these

9.7. is the beauty of the woman." So, taking her by the hand, he led her out, and then, calling his confederate, he said, "Look—here is the divinity you were afraid of. A fine pirate you are, to be frightened by a woman. You, then, guard her; for I wish to give her back to her parents. We will carry out what is stored inside, now that not even the dead woman is keeping it any longer."

10.1. When they had filled the cutter with the spoils, Theron ordered the guard to withdraw a little with the woman; then he put before them a deliberation about her. And their opinions were divided and at variance with one another.

10.2. For the first to speak said, "We came for other ends, comrades, but something better has befallen us from fortune; let us make use of it, for we can do the thing without danger. I propose that we leave the grave-offerings where they are, but give Callirhoe back to her husband and father, saying that we put in at this place by our usual fishing custom, and hearing a voice we opened the tomb out of humanity, to save the woman shut up inside.

10.3. Let us make the woman swear to bear witness to everything for us. She will gladly do it, owing gratitude to her benefactors, through whom she was saved. With how much joy do you think we will fill all Sicily? How many gifts will we receive? And at the same time we will be doing what is just toward men and pious toward the gods."

10.4. While he was still speaking, another contradicted him: "Untimely fool, do you now bid us play the philosopher? Has tomb-robbing made us virtuous? Shall we pity her whom her own husband did not pity but killed? For she has done us no wrong;

10.5. but she will do us the greatest wrong. For, first, if we give her back to her relatives, it is uncertain what view they will take of what has happened, and it is impossible that the reason we came to the tomb should not be suspected. And even if the woman's kinsmen grant us pardon, still the magistrates and the people themselves will not let off tomb-robbers who bring against themselves the evidence of their crime.

10.6. Perhaps someone will say it is more profitable to sell the woman, for we will find a price for her because of her beauty. But this too has its danger. Gold has no voice, nor will the silver say where we got it; for these we can invent a story.

10.7. But a piece of cargo that has eyes and ears and a tongue—who could keep that hidden? And the beauty, besides, is not human, so that we could escape notice. When we say she is a slave, who that has seen her will believe it? Let us kill her here, then, and not carry about with us the witness against ourselves."

10.8. When many agreed with these men, Theron put neither opinion to the vote. "You," he said, "bring on danger; and you throw away profit. But I will sell the woman rather than destroy her; for when she is being sold she will keep silent out of fear, but once sold let her accuse those who are not present. Come, embark; let us sail; for it is already near day."

11.1. The ship put out and ran on splendidly; for they did not have to struggle against wave and wind, since they had no particular course set before them, but every wind seemed favorable to them and stood astern. Theron tried to comfort Callirhoe, attempting to deceive her with various devices.

11.2. But she understood her own situation and that she had been saved to no purpose; yet she pretended not to understand but to believe him, fearing that they might even kill her if she seemed angry. Saying that she could not bear the sea, she covered her face and wept, and said, "You, father, in this very sea defeated three hundred ships of the Athenians, yet a little cutter has carried off your daughter, and you give me no help.

11.3. I am being taken to a foreign land, and I, the well-born, must be a slave; and perhaps some Athenian master will buy the daughter of Hermocrates. How much better it would have been for me to lie dead in the tomb! At least Chaereas would have been buried with me; but as it is, both living and dead we have been parted."

11.4. So she was in such laments, while the pirates sailed past little islands and cities; for the cargo was not of the poor, and they were looking for wealthy men. They put in opposite Attica, under a headland; there was a spring there of much pure water, and a fine meadow.

11.5. There they brought Callirhoe out and bade her freshen herself and rest a little from the sea, wishing to preserve her beauty; and by themselves they deliberated where they should direct their voyage. And one of them said, "Athens is near, a great and prosperous city. There we will find a multitude of merchants and a multitude of rich men. For just as in a marketplace one sees men, so in Athens one sees cities." It seemed good to all to sail into Athens,

11.6. but Theron did not like the meddlesomeness of the city. "Are you alone unaware," he said, "of the inquisitiveness of the Athenians? They are a talkative and litigious people, and in the harbor a thousand informers will ask who we are and where we are carrying this cargo from. A wicked suspicion will seize the malicious.

11.7. The Areopagus is right there, and magistrates harsher than tyrants. Let us fear the Athenians more than the Syracusans. A suitable place for us is Ionia, for there is royal wealth there, flowing down from greater Asia above, and the people are luxurious and free from care; and I expect to find some acquaintances there too."

11.8. So, having taken on water and provisions from the merchant ships at anchor, they sailed straight for Miletus, and on the third day they put in at an anchorage eighty stades distant from the city, very well suited for a landing.

12.1. There Theron ordered the oars to be carried out and a resting-place to be made for Callirhoe, and everything provided for her comfort. This he did not out of kindness but out of greed for gain, as a merchant rather than a pirate. He himself hurried off to the town, taking two of his companions with him. Then he did not openly set about looking for a buyer or making the matter notorious, but secretly and underhandedly he pressed on with the sale. It proved hard to manage; for the property was not one for many men, nor for any ordinary buyer, but for some rich man, even a king, and he was afraid to approach such people.

12.2. So as the delay grew longer, he could no longer endure the procrastination; and when night came on he could not sleep, but said to himself, "You are a fool, Theron; for you have now left silver and gold for so many days in a deserted place, as though you were the only pirate.

12.3. Do you not know that other pirates also sail the sea? And I am afraid of our own men, lest they abandon us and sail away; for surely you did not enlist the most honest of men, to keep faith with you, but the most wicked you knew.

12.4. For now," he said, "go to sleep, of necessity; but when day comes, run down to the cutter and throw into the sea this woman who is unseasonable and superfluous to you, and no longer take aboard a cargo that is hard to dispose of." But when he slept, he saw in a dream the doors locked.
12.5. So he decided to wait that day. And as he idled about, he sat at a workshop, his soul thoroughly troubled.

12.6. Meanwhile a throng of people went by, free men and slaves, and in the midst of them a man of mature age, dressed in black and gloomy. So Theron rose—for man's nature is inquisitive—and asked one of the attendants, "Who is this?" And the man answered, "You seem to me to be a stranger or to have come from far off, since you do not know Dionysius, who surpasses the other Ionians in wealth and birth and culture, a friend of the great King."

12.7. "Why, then, is he in black?" "Because his wife, whom he loved, has died." Theron clung the more to the conversation, having found a rich man fond of women. So he would not let the man go, but asked,

12.8. "What position do you hold with him?" And he answered, "I am steward of all his affairs, and I raise his daughter for him too, a young child, an infant orphaned before her time of her wretched mother." "What is your name?" "Leonas." "Opportunely, Leonas," he said, "have I met you. I am a merchant, and I am now sailing from Italy, so that I know nothing of affairs in Ionia. A woman of Sybaris, the most prosperous of the people there, owned a most beautiful maid and sold her out of jealousy, and I bought her.

12.9. The profit, then, shall be yours, whether you wish to keep her for yourself as nurse for the child—for she is well enough educated—or whether you think it worthy to make a gift of her to your master. It is more to your advantage that he should have a bought slave,

12.10. so that he may not bring in a stepmother for your foster-child." Leonas heard this gladly and said, "Some god has sent you down as my benefactor; for you show me in waking what I have been dreaming of. Come, then, to the house, and become at once my friend and guest; and the choice about the woman, whether the property is one for a master or for the likes of us, the sight of her shall decide."
13.1. When they came to the house, Theron marveled at its size and costliness—for it was furnished for the reception of the King of Persia—but Leonas bade him wait while he first attended to

13.2. the service of his master. Then, taking the man, he led him up to his own quarters, which were very gentlemanly, and ordered a table to be set. And Theron, like the scoundrel he was, skilled at adapting himself to every occasion, fell to the food and showed Leonas his goodwill with toasts, partly as a display of his frankness,

13.3. but more for the sake of partnership and trust. Meanwhile there was much conversation about the woman, and Theron praised the woman's character rather than her beauty, knowing that what is unseen needs advocacy, while the sight commends itself. "Let us go, then,"

13.4. said Leonas, "and show her to me." But he answered, "She is not here; for because of the customs-officers we kept clear of the city, and the ship lies eighty stades off," and he described the place. "It is in our own lands that you have anchored," he said, "and this is the better, since fortune is already leading you to Dionysius.
13.5. Let us go off, then, to the country estate, so that you may also recover yourselves from the sea; for the nearby villa has been built at great cost." Theron was the more pleased,

13.6. thinking the sale would be easier not in the marketplace but in a lonely place, and he said, "At dawn let us go off, you to the villa, I to the ship, and from there I will bring the woman to you." They agreed on this and, clasping right hands with each other, parted. To both the night seemed long, the one eager to buy, the other to sell.

13.7. On the next day Leonas sailed along to the villa, bringing silver as well, so that he might secure the merchant beforehand; and Theron came to the shore and to his confederates, who longed for him greatly, and having told them the business, he began to coax Callirhoe.

13.8. "I myself, daughter," he said, "wished at once to take you back to your own people; but a contrary wind arose and I was prevented by the sea. You know what care I have taken of you; and, the greatest thing, we have kept you pure. Chaereas will receive you unviolated, saved by us from the tomb as from a bridal chamber.

13.9. Now, then, it is necessary for us to run as far as Lycia; but it is not necessary that you too should suffer hardship in vain, and that being so seasick. Here, then, I will place you with faithful friends, and on my return I will take you back and with great care bring you at last to Syracuse. Take of your own whatever you wish; for the rest, too, we are keeping for you."

13.10. At this Callirhoe laughed to herself, though she was deeply grieved, and thought him an utter fool; for she knew already that she was being sold, yet she counted the sale a happier thing than her former noble state, wishing to be rid of the pirates. And she said, "I thank you, father, for your kindness toward me; and may the gods repay you all your due rewards.

13.11. But to use the grave-offerings I think ill-omened. Keep them all safe for me; for me a little ring is enough, which I had even when dead." Then, covering her head, she said, "Take me, Theron, wherever you wish; for any place is better than the sea and the tomb."

14.1. When Theron came near the villa, he devised something of this kind. Uncovering Callirhoe and loosing her hair, he opened the door and ordered her to go in first. Leonas and all those inside, when she appeared suddenly, were astonished, thinking they had seen a goddess; for there was a report in the countryside that Aphrodite showed herself there.

14.2. While they were thus astounded, Theron, following behind, came up to Leonas and said, "Rise and see to the reception of the woman; for this is she you wish to buy." Joy and wonder followed in all of them.

14.3. So they laid Callirhoe down in the finest of the rooms and let her rest; for she needed much repose after grief and toil and fear. And Theron, taking Leonas's right hand, said, "On my side everything has been faithfully fulfilled; do you now have the woman—for you are my friend henceforth—and come to the city and take the deed of sale, and then pay me the price,

14.4. whatever you wish." Wishing to make a return, Leonas said, "No, rather I too entrust the silver to you now, before the deed of sale," and at the same time he wished to secure the deal in advance, fearing that he might change his mind; for, he thought, there would be many in the city wanting to buy her.

14.5. So bringing out a talent of silver, he forced him to take it, and Theron, after some affected reluctance, took it. When Leonas was detaining him for dinner—for it was late in the day—he said, "I wish to sail to the city this evening, and tomorrow we will meet at the harbor."

14.6. On these terms they parted. Coming to the ship, Theron ordered the men to weigh anchor and put out as quickly as possible, before they should be discovered. And so they were running away wherever the wind carried them, and Callirhoe, now alone and at liberty, lamented her own fortune. "See," she said, "another tomb, in which Theron has shut me up, more desolate than the first;

14.7. for there my father might have come to me, and my mother, and Chaereas might have poured a libation with his tears; I would have known it even though dead. But whom shall I call upon here? You know it, envious Fortune. Through land and sea you have not been satisfied with my misfortunes, but first you made my lover my murderer—Chaereas, who never struck even a slave, gave me, who loved him, a mortal kick;

14.8. then you handed me into the hands of tomb-robbers and led me out of the tomb into the sea and set over me pirates more fearful than the waves. And this far-famed beauty I acquired only that Theron the pirate might get a great price for me.

14.9. In a deserted place I have been sold, and I was not even brought into a city, like other bought slaves; for you were afraid, Fortune, that someone seeing me might think me well-born. For this reason I have been handed over like a piece of goods I know not to whom—Greeks or barbarians or pirates again." Beating her breast with her hand, she saw on the ring the likeness of Chaereas, and kissing it she said, "Truly I am lost,

14.10. Chaereas, parted from you by so great a calamity. And you mourn and repent and sit beside an empty tomb, bearing witness after my death to my chastity, while I, the daughter of Hermocrates, your wife, have today been sold to a master." As she lamented thus, sleep at last came over her.

1.1. Leonas, having ordered Phocas the steward to take great care of the woman, set out himself while it was still night for Miletus, eager to bring his master the good news about the newly bought slave, thinking it would bring him great consolation in his grief. He found Dionysius still lying abed; for, distracted by his sorrow, he hardly went out, though his country longed for him, but stayed in his chamber as though his wife were still with him.

1.2. Seeing Leonas, he said to him, "This one night, since the death of that poor woman, I have slept sweetly; for I saw her plainly, grown taller and lovelier, and she was with me as in waking life. I thought it was the first day of our wedding and that I was bringing her as a bride from my estates by the sea, while you sang the wedding-hymn for me." While he was still telling this,

1.3. Leonas cried out, "You are fortunate, master, both in dream and in waking life. You are about to hear of the very things you have beheld." And beginning his account, he said, "A merchant came to me selling a most beautiful woman, but because of the customs-officers he anchored his ship outside the city, near your estates.
1.4. And I, having made the agreement, went off to the country. There, when we had come together, we as good as completed the sale; for I gave him a talent. But the deed of sale must be drawn up here

1.5. according to law." Dionysius was glad to hear of the woman's beauty—for he was truly fond of women—but was displeased at her slavery; for being a man of royal rank, surpassing all Ionia in dignity and culture, he disdained the bed of a maidservant, and said, "It is impossible, Leonas, that a beautiful body should not be of free birth. Do you not hear the poets, that the beautiful are children of the gods, and long before that of well-born men? She pleased you in a lonely place, for you compared her with the country women.

1.6. But since you have bought her, go to the marketplace; Adrastus, the man most experienced in the laws, will arrange the deeds of sale." Leonas was glad to be disbelieved; for the unexpected would strike his master the more. Going about all the harbors of Miletus and the banks and the whole city, he could nowhere find Theron.

1.7. He questioned merchants and ferrymen, but no one knew him. Then, in great perplexity, he took a rowing boat and sailed along to the shore and from there to the estate; but he was not likely to find the man who was already at sea. So at last, slowly and reluctantly, he went off to his master.

1.8. Dionysius, seeing him gloomy, asked what had happened to him; and he said, "I have lost you a talent, master." "That happening," said Dionysius, "will make you more careful for the future. But what has happened? Has the newly bought slave run away?" "Not she," he said, "but the man who sold her." "He was a kidnapper, then, and that is why he sold you another man's slave in a lonely place.

1.9. Where did he say the woman was from?" "From Sybaris in Italy, sold by her mistress out of jealousy." "Find out whether any people from Sybaris are in town; and in the meantime leave the woman there." So Leonas went off grieving, thinking his enterprise had not turned out well; and he watched for an opportunity to persuade his master to go out to the estates, having now one hope left—the sight of the woman.

2.1. The country women came in to Callirhoe and at once began to flatter her as their mistress. Plangon, the steward's wife, no idle creature, said to her, "You are surely longing, my child, for your own people; but believe that here too you have your own; for Dionysius, our master, is good and kind. By good fortune the god has brought you into a good house.

2.2. You will live as in your own country. So wash off the salt from the long voyage; you have maidservants." With difficulty, and against her will, she nevertheless brought her to the bath. When she went in, they anointed and cleansed her with care, and when she undressed they were the more astonished; so that, having admired her face while she was clothed, they thought they were now looking on a divine face. For her skin shone, white, with a kind of radiance, gleaming; and her flesh was so tender that they were afraid even the touch of their fingers might make a great wound.

2.3. They whispered quietly to one another, "Beautiful and famous indeed is our mistress; but this one might have passed for her maid." The praise grieved Callirhoe, and she was not without foreboding of what was to come. When she had bathed and they were binding up her hair, they brought her clean garments; but she said these were not fitting for a newly bought slave.
2.4. "Give me a slave's tunic; for you too are better than I am." So she put on something ordinary; and even that became her and seemed costly, lit up as it was by her beauty.

2.5. When the women had eaten, Plangon said, "Come to Aphrodite and pray for yourself; the goddess is manifest here, and not only the neighbors but those who come from the city sacrifice to her. Above all she gives ear to Dionysius; he has never

2.6. passed her by." Then they told of the goddess's manifestations, and one of the country women said, "You will think, woman, when you behold Aphrodite, that you are looking at an image of yourself." When Callirhoe heard this she was filled with tears and said to herself, "Alas for my misfortune! Here too is the goddess Aphrodite, the cause of all my evils. Yet I will go, for I wish to make many complaints to her."

2.7. The temple was near the villa, beside the highway itself. Callirhoe made obeisance and, taking hold of the feet of Aphrodite, said, "You first showed me Chaereas; but having joined a beautiful pair, you did not keep them so—and yet we honored you.

2.8. Since, then, you have willed it so, I ask one favor of you: make me please no man after him." To this Aphrodite refused her assent; for she is the mother of Love, and she was contriving yet another marriage—one which she did not mean to keep either.
Now that Callirhoe was free of pirates and the sea, she recovered her own beauty, so that the country people marveled to see her growing lovelier day by day.

3.1. Leonas, having found a suitable moment, brought such words to Dionysius: "It is now a long time, master, since you went to your estates by the sea, and the people there long for your presence. You must inspect the herds and the plantations, and the gathering of the crops presses on.

3.2. Enjoy too the costliness of the houses which we built at your bidding; and you will bear your grief more lightly there, drawn off by the pleasure and management of the lands. And if you commend some herdsman or shepherd, you may give him the newly bought woman." This pleased Dionysius, and he appointed the day for the journey.

3.3. When the order was given, the charioteers prepared the carriages, the grooms the horses, the sailors the ferryboats; friends were invited to travel with him, and a crowd of freedmen; for Dionysius was by nature magnificent.

3.4. When everything was ready, he ordered the equipage and the greater part of the company to go by sea, and the carriages to follow when he himself had gone ahead; for, he said, a procession was not fitting for a man in mourning. At dawn, before the multitude noticed, he mounted his horse, and Leonas was one of the five with him.

3.5. So Dionysius rode out to the country; and Callirhoe, having beheld Aphrodite that night, wished to make obeisance to her again. She stood praying, while Dionysius, leaping down from his horse, was the first to enter the temple. Hearing the sound of footsteps, Callirhoe turned toward him.

3.6. Then Dionysius, beholding her, cried out, "Be gracious, Aphrodite, and appear to me for my good." As he was already sinking down, Leonas caught him and said, "This, master, is the newly bought slave; be not at all disturbed. And you, woman, come forward to your lord." At the word "lord" Callirhoe let fall a stream of tears, bowing her head down, learning her servitude at last and unwillingly; and Dionysius, striking Leonas, said, "Most impious of men, do you speak to the gods as to human beings?
3.7. Do you say that this woman was bought with silver and that you could not find the seller? Have you not heard even Homer teaching us:

And the gods, in the likeness of strangers from afar,
look upon the violence and the good order of men.
. . . "At least from now on stop mocking me and thinking that one is a god who is not even a fortunate human being."

3.8. As she spoke, her voice seemed to Dionysius something divine; for it sounded musical and gave back a tone like a lyre's. At a loss, then, and ashamed to converse further, he went off to the villa, already inflamed with love. Not long after, the equipage came from the city, and a swift report of what had happened ran abroad.

3.9. So all hurried to see the woman, but all pretended to be worshipping Aphrodite. Callirhoe, abashed at the crowd, did not know what to do; for everything was strange to her, and she could not even see her familiar Plangon, who was busy about the reception of the master.

3.10. As the hour advanced and no one came to the villa, but all stood there as if spellbound, Leonas understood what had happened and, coming to the precinct, led Callirhoe out. Then one might see that there are men who are kings by nature, as in a swarm of bees; for all followed her, as if by reason of her beauty she had been elected their mistress.

4.1. So she went off to her usual lodging; but Dionysius had been wounded and tried to conceal the wound. As a man of education and one who especially laid claim to virtue, unwilling to seem contemptible to his servants or boyish to his friends, he held out through the whole evening, thinking himself unobserved, but betrayed by his very silence.

4.2. Taking some portion from his dinner, he said, "Let someone carry this to the stranger-woman. But do not say it is from her lord, but that it is from Dionysius." He prolonged the drinking as much as possible; for he knew he was not going to sleep. He wished, then, to keep wakeful with his friends.

4.3. When the night was far advanced, he broke up the party; but sleep did not fall to his lot, and he was wholly in the temple of Aphrodite, recalling everything—her face, her hair, how she turned, how she looked at him, her voice, her bearing, her words; and her tears too inflamed him.

4.4. Then one might have seen a contest between reason and passion. For though plunged beneath his desire, the noble man tried to resist, and, as if from a wave, he kept lifting his head, saying to himself, "Are you not ashamed, Dionysius, you the first man of Ionia for virtue and renown, whom satraps and kings and cities admire, to suffer the troubles of a boy? Once you have seen her, you are in love—and that while in mourning, before you have made the rites for the spirits of your poor wife.

4.5. Was it for this that you came to the country, to celebrate a wedding in black, and the wedding of a slave at that—perhaps even another man's? For you do not even have the deed of sale for her." But Love strove against him as he reasoned well, and counted his self-control an outrage; and for this reason he burned the more fiercely a soul that played the philosopher in love.

4.6. No longer able, then, to endure conversing with himself alone, he sent for Leonas; and when he was summoned, Leonas understood the cause but pretended ignorance, and as if disturbed said, "Why are you awake, master? Has some grief over your dead wife laid hold of you again?" "Over a woman," said Dionysius, "but not over the dead one. I keep nothing secret from you, because of your goodwill and faith.

4.7. You have ruined me, Leonas. You are the cause of my troubles. You have brought fire into the house, or rather into my soul. And what disturbs me is the uncertainty about the woman. You tell me a tale of a winged merchant, of whom you know neither where he came from nor where he went off to again. Who is it that, having such beauty, sells in a lonely place for a talent what is worth a king's wealth? Some divinity has deceived you.

4.8. Take heed, then, and recall what happened. Whom did you see? With whom did you speak? Tell me the truth. You did not behold a ship." "I did not see one, master, but I heard of one." "There it is: one of the Nymphs or Nereids has come up out of the sea. There are times appointed by fate which bring even divinities under the necessity of consorting with men; the poets and historians tell us this."

4.9. Dionysius was glad to persuade himself to exalt the woman and to think her more venerable than belonged to human company. And Leonas, wishing to gratify his master, said, "Let us not inquire too curiously, master, who she is; I will bring her to you, if you wish, and have no grief. Are you failing

4.10. when you have the power of love?" "I will not do it," said Dionysius, "before I learn who the woman is and where she is from. At dawn, then, let us learn the truth from her. But I will summon her not here, lest we incur the suspicion of some violence, but where I first beheld her; let our conversation take place at the temple of Aphrodite."

5.1. This was resolved; and on the next day Dionysius, taking with him friends and freedmen and the most trusted of his servants, so that he might have witnesses too, came to the precinct, having arranged himself not carelessly, but adorning his person quietly, as one about to converse with the woman he loved.

5.2. He was by nature handsome and tall, and above all most dignified to look upon. Leonas, taking Plangon and with her the maidservants familiar to Callirhoe, came to her and said, "Dionysius is a most just and law-abiding man.

5.3. Come, then, to the temple, woman, and tell him the truth, who you are; for you will not fail of any just help. Only speak to him simply, and hide nothing of the truth; for this will the more call forth his kindness toward you." So Callirhoe walked unwillingly, yet taking courage because their conversation was to take place in a temple.

5.4. When she came, they all admired her still more. Dionysius, struck dumb, was speechless. After a long silence, at last and with difficulty he spoke: "My circumstances, woman, are all plain to you. I am Dionysius, the first man of the Milesians, and of nearly all Ionia, renowned for piety and kindness.

5.5. It is just that you too should tell us the truth about yourself; for those who sold you said you were from Sybaris, sold from there by your mistress out of jealousy." Callirhoe blushed and, bowing her head down, said quietly, "I am now sold for the first time; I have never seen Sybaris."

5.6. "I told you," said Dionysius, looking toward Leonas, "that she is no slave; and I divine that she is well-born too. Tell me everything, woman, and first your name." "Callirhoe," she said—and the name too pleased Dionysius—but the rest she kept silent. When he questioned her insistently, she said, "I beg you, master, allow me to keep silent about my fortune.

5.7. The first part was a dream and a tale; I am now what I have become, a slave and a stranger." As she said this she tried to hide it, but her tears flowed down her cheeks; and Dionysius was moved to weep, and all who stood around; and one might have thought that even Aphrodite herself had grown sadder. But Dionysius pressed her still more, inquiring closely, and said, "This favor I ask of you first.

5.8. Tell me your own story, Callirhoe. You will not be telling it to a stranger; for there is a kinship of character too. Fear nothing, even if you have done something dreadful." Callirhoe was indignant at this and said, "Do not insult me;

5.9. for I am conscious of nothing base in myself. But since my own affairs are more dignified than my present fortune, I do not wish to seem a boaster, nor to tell tales beyond belief to those who do not know me; for what went before does not bear witness to what is now." Dionysius admired the spirit of the woman and said, "I understand already, even though you do not speak; yet speak nevertheless. For you will tell nothing about yourself so great as what we see.

5.10. Any account is less brilliant than you are." So at last she began to tell her story: "I am the daughter of Hermocrates, the general of the Syracusans. Having fallen speechless from a sudden swoon, I was buried by my parents at great cost. Tomb-robbers opened the tomb; they found me breathing again; they brought me here, and Theron handed me over to this man Leonas in a lonely place." Telling all, she kept silent only about Chaereas.

5.11. "But I beg you, Dionysius—for you are a Greek, and have a share in a kindly city and in culture—do not become like the tomb-robbers, nor rob me of my country and kindred. It is a small thing for you, who are wealthy, to release one person; you will not lose the price if you give me back to my father; Hermocrates is not ungrateful. We all admire and love Alcinous because he sent the suppliant back to his country. I too entreat you.

5.12. Save a captive orphan girl. If I cannot live as a free woman, I choose a free death." Hearing this, he wept, on the pretext of Callirhoe, but in truth for himself; for he perceived that he was failing of his desire. "Take courage, Callirhoe," he said, "and have a good heart; for you will not fail of what you ask; I call this Aphrodite to witness. But in the meantime you shall have attendance among us as a mistress rather than a slave."

6.1. So she went off, persuaded that she could suffer nothing against her will; but Dionysius, grieving, came to his own house and, calling Leonas alone, said, "In everything I am unfortunate and hated by Love. I have buried my wife, and the newly bought slave is fleeing me—she whom I hoped was a gift to me from Aphrodite, and I was fashioning for myself a blessed life beyond Menelaus's, the husband of the Spartan woman; for I do not suppose that even Helen was so beautiful.

6.2. And she has too the persuasiveness of speech. My life is over. On the same day Callirhoe shall depart from here and I from life." At this Leonas cried out, "Do not, master, do not curse yourself; for you are her lord and have power over her, so that, willing or unwilling, she will do what seems good to you;

6.3. for I bought her for a talent." "You bought, you thrice-wretched man, the well-born woman? Do you not hear of Hermocrates, the general of all Sicily, greatly celebrated, whom the King of the Persians admires and loves, and to whom he sends gifts every year because he defeated in a sea-battle the Athenians, the enemies of the Persians? Shall I play the tyrant over a free body, and shall Dionysius, famed for self-control, outrage against her will one whom not even Theron the pirate outraged?"

6.4. This, then, he said to Leonas; yet he did not despair of persuading her—for love is by nature full of hope—and he trusted to win his desire by attendance and service. So calling Plangon, he said, "You have already given me sufficient proof of your care. I now put into your hands the greatest and most precious of my possessions, the stranger-woman. I wish her to lack nothing, but to go forward even to luxury.

6.5. Regard her as your mistress, serve and adorn her and make her a friend to us; praise me to her often, and tell of me as you know how. See that you do not call me master." Plangon understood the command, for she was by nature quick-witted; and at once turning her mind to the matter, she set off to it. Coming, then, to Callirhoe, she did not reveal that she had been ordered to serve her, but showed her own goodwill; and she wished to have her trust as a counselor.

7.1. And something of this kind occurred. Dionysius lingered in the country, on various pretexts at different times, but the truth was that he could neither part from Callirhoe nor was willing to bring her in; for once seen she was bound to become famous, and her beauty would enslave all Ionia, and the report of her would rise even to the great King.

7.2. While he stayed there, inquiring more closely into the management of the property, he found some fault with the steward Phocas; but the blame went no further, only to words. Plangon found her opportunity and ran in terrified to Callirhoe, tearing her own hair; and taking hold of her knees she said, "I beg you, mistress, save us; for Dionysius is angry with my husband; he is by nature quick-tempered, just as he is kind.

7.3. No one could rescue us but you alone; for Dionysius will gladly grant you a first favor when you ask it." Callirhoe hesitated to go to him; but as Plangon persisted and entreated, she could not refuse, being already pledged by the kindnesses done her by the woman. So that she might not seem ungrateful, she said, "I too am a slave and have no freedom of speech; but if you suppose that I too can be of some use, I am ready to join in entreaty; and may we succeed." When they came,

7.4. Plangon ordered the doorkeeper to announce to the master that Callirhoe was present. Dionysius happened to be lying prostrate with grief, and his body too was wasted. Hearing, then, that Callirhoe was present, he was struck dumb, and a kind of mist poured over him at the unexpected news; but barely recovering, he said, "Let her come."

7.5. Callirhoe, standing near and bowing her head down, was first filled with blushes, but at last with difficulty she spoke: "I owe gratitude to this Plangon; for she loves me as a daughter. I beg you, lord, do not be angry with her husband, but grant their safety."

7.6. Wishing to say more, she could not. So Dionysius, understanding the stratagem of Plangon, said, "I am angry, and no man could have saved Phocas and Plangon from perishing for what they did; but I grant them to you gladly, and know, you two, that for Callirhoe's sake you have been saved." Plangon fell at his knees, and Dionysius said, "Fall at Callirhoe's knees,

7.7. for it is she who saved you." When Plangon saw that Callirhoe was glad and greatly pleased at the gift, she said, "Then do you confess gratitude to Dionysius on our behalf," and at the same time she pushed her. And she, falling forward in a way, came against the right hand of Dionysius, and he, as if disdaining to give his hand, drew her to him and kissed her, then at once let her go, lest any suspicion of the trick should arise.

8.1. So the women went off, but the kiss sank like poison into the vitals of Dionysius, and he could neither see nor hear any longer, but was besieged on every side, finding no remedy for his love—neither by gifts, for he saw the woman's high-mindedness, nor by threat or force, being convinced that she would choose death sooner than be forced. So he supposed Plangon his one help, and summoning her he said, "Your first measures have been well managed, and I thank you for the kiss;

8.2. but that has either saved me or destroyed me. Consider, then, how, woman against woman, you may prevail, having me too for an ally. And know that freedom is set before you as a prize, and—what I am sure is far sweeter to you than freedom—the life of Dionysius." So Plangon, thus ordered, brought to bear every effort and device; but Callirhoe was on every side unconquered, and remained faithful to Chaereas alone.

8.3. Yet she was outgeneraled by fortune, against which alone human reasoning avails nothing; for that divinity is fond of strife, and nothing is past hope with her. And so at that time too she accomplished a strange thing, or rather an incredible one; and the manner of it is worth hearing.

8.4. Fortune plotted against the woman's chastity. For Chaereas and Callirhoe, having made the first union of their marriage a thing of passion, had felt a like impulse toward the enjoyment of each other, and a balanced desire made their intercourse not barren.

8.5. So a little before her fall the woman conceived. But because of the dangers and hardships that followed, she did not quickly realize that she had become pregnant; but as the third month began, her belly grew; and in the bath Plangon understood, as one who had experience of women's matters.

8.6. At first she kept silent, because of the number of the maidservants; but toward evening, when there was leisure, sitting beside her on the couch she said, "Know, my child, that you are with child." Callirhoe broke into weeping and, wailing and tearing her hair, said, "This too, Fortune, you have added to my misfortunes, that I should bear

8.7. a slave." And striking her belly she said, "Wretched, you have become wretched before you were born; you have been delivered into a tomb and the hands of pirates. Into what kind of life are you coming? On what hopes am I to carry you, orphaned and without a country and a slave? Before your birth, make trial of death." Plangon held her hands and promised that on the next day she would prepare for her an easier abortion.

9.1. Each of the women, when she was by herself, took her own counsel: Plangon, that a suitable moment had appeared for accomplishing her master's love, having the child in the womb as advocate—"a pledge of persuasion has been found; a mother's tenderness will conquer a woman's chastity." And so she put together the plan plausibly;

9.2. while Callirhoe deliberated about destroying the child, saying to herself, "Shall I, then, bear to a master the descendant of Hermocrates, and bring forth a child whose father no one knows? Perhaps one of those who envy me will say, 'In the pirates' den Callirhoe conceived.' It is enough that I alone should be unfortunate.

9.3. It is not to your advantage, child, to come into a wretched life, which even at birth you ought to flee. Depart free, untouched by evils. Hear none of the tales about your mother." But again she changed her mind, and somehow pity for the child within her came over her. "Are you planning to kill your own child, most impious of all women, and taking on the reasonings of Medea?

9.4. Why, you will seem wilder even than the Scythian woman; for she had her husband as an enemy, but you wish to kill the child of Chaereas and to leave behind not even a memorial of your celebrated marriage. What if it is a son? What if it is like its father? What if it is more fortunate than I? Shall a mother kill the one saved from the tomb and from pirates?

9.5. How many children of gods and kings do we hear of, born in slavery, who afterward recovered the rank of their fathers—Zethus and Amphion and Cyrus? You too, child, shall sail with me to Sicily; you shall seek out your father and grandfather and tell them your mother's story. A fleet shall be brought out from there to help me.
9.6. You, child, shall give back the parents to each other." As she reasoned thus through the whole night, sleep came over her for a little while. And the likeness of Chaereas stood beside her,

resembling him in everything, in stature and in beautiful eyes,
and in voice, and such garments was he clothed about his body.

And standing he said, "I commit my son to you, woman." While he still wished to speak, Callirhoe started up, wishing to embrace him. So, considering her husband her counselor, she resolved to rear the child.

10.1. On the next day, when Plangon came, she made known to her her decision. But Plangon did not accept the unseasonableness of the plan, and said, "It is impossible for you, woman, to rear a child among us; for our master, being disposed to you with love, will not force you against your will, out of respect and self-control, but will not permit you to rear a child, out of jealousy, thinking himself insulted if you hold the absent man in such regard but slight him when he is present.

10.2. It seems to me, then, better that the child should perish before its birth than after. For so you will be spared useless labor-pains and a fruitless pregnancy. And I, loving you, give you true counsel." Callirhoe heard this with grief, and falling at her knees she begged her to help find some device

10.3. by which she might rear the child. So, after many refusals, putting off her answer for two or three days, when she had inflamed Callirhoe the more toward entreaty and made herself the more to be trusted, she first made her swear to tell no one of the device, and then, knitting her brows and rubbing her hands, said, "Great matters, woman, are brought to success by great contrivances; and I, because of my goodwill toward you, will betray my master.

10.4. Know, then, that one of two things must be: either the child must perish utterly, or be born the wealthiest of the Ionians, heir of the most brilliant house. And he will make you, his mother, blessed. Choose, then, which you wish." "And who," she said, "would be so foolish as to choose the killing of her child instead of happiness? But you seem to me to be saying something impossible and incredible, so make it plainer."

10.5. Plangon then asked, "How long do you think it is since you conceived?" And she said, "Two months." "Time, then, is on our side; for you can seem to have borne to Dionysius a seven-months child." At this Callirhoe cried out,

10.6. "Rather let it perish." And Plangon spoke mockingly to her: "You are right, woman, to wish rather to miscarry. Let us do this; for it is less dangerous than to deceive a master. Cut off from yourself on every side the tokens of your noble birth,

10.7. and let there be no hope of your country. Adapt yourself to your present fortune and become wholly a slave." As Plangon urged this, Callirhoe suspected nothing, a girl of noble birth and inexperienced in the cunning of slaves; but the more eagerly Plangon pressed for the destruction of the child, the more Callirhoe pitied the one in her womb, and said, "Give me time for reflection; for the choice is about the greatest things,

10.8. either my chastity or my child." Again Plangon praised this, that she did not rashly choose either; "for the inclination to each side is persuasive: the one has a woman's faithfulness, the other a mother's tenderness. Yet there is no time for long delay, but on the next day you must by all means hold to one or the other, before your pregnancy becomes known." They agreed on this and parted from each other.

11.1. Going up to the upper chamber and shutting the doors, Callirhoe set the likeness of Chaereas against her belly and said, "See, we have become three—husband and wife and child. Let us take counsel about what is for the common good. I, then, am the first to declare my opinion: I wish to die the wife of Chaereas alone. This is sweeter to me than parents and country and child—to take no trial of another husband.

11.2. But you, child, on your own behalf, what do you choose? To die by poison before you have seen the sun, and to be cast out with your mother, perhaps not even thought worthy of burial—or to live and have two fathers, the one the first man of Sicily, the other of Ionia? When you become a man you will easily be recognized by your kindred; for I am sure I shall bear you like your father; and you shall sail home gloriously on a Milesian trireme, and Hermocrates will gladly receive a grandson

11.3. already able to be a general. You cast against me, child, a contrary vote, and do not allow us to die. Let us ask your father too. Or rather he has already spoken; for he himself, standing beside me in my dreams, said, 'I commit my son to you.' I call you to witness, Chaereas:

11.4. you are giving me as a bride to Dionysius." So through that day and night she was in these reflections, and not for her own sake but for the infant's she was persuaded to live; and on the next day Plangon came, and first sat down gloomy and showed a sympathetic bearing,

11.5. and there was silence between them both. When a long time had passed, Plangon asked, "What have you decided? What are we to do? For there is no time for delay." Callirhoe could not answer quickly, weeping and confused, but at last she said, "The child betrays me against my will; do you do what is expedient; but I am afraid that, even if I submit to the outrage, Dionysius may despise my fortune and, thinking me a concubine rather than a wife, may not rear the child born of another,

11.6. and I shall have lost my chastity in vain." While she was still speaking, Plangon broke in and said, "I myself have considered these things before you; for I already love you more than my master. I trust, then, in the character of Dionysius, for he is good; yet I will make him swear an oath, even though he is master; we must do everything safely. And you too, child, see that you make a return. But I will go and carry the embassy."
